theme: The divine nature; the prophetic word confirmed
readingInstruction: Read 2 Peter 1:1-21. This letter is Peter’s last testimony, written as his death approaches. Notice the great promises, the call to grow, and the confidence he gives in the apostolic witness and the prophetic word.
settingTheScene: Peter writes his second letter shortly before his martyrdom, probably in the mid-60s AD. He knows that “the putting off of my body will be soon” (1:14), just as the Lord Jesus told him. His readers are in danger of false teachers who would draw them from the truth, so Peter wants to remind them of what they know. He calls himself Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle, and begins with the foundation of the whole Christian life: what God has already given us in Christ.
observation: “To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours” (1:1).
“His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness” (1:3).
“That through them you may become partakers of the divine nature” (1:4).
“Make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue” (1:5).
“Be all the more diligent to make your calling and election sure” (1:10).
“For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty” (1:16).
“And we have something more sure, the prophetic word, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (1:19).
“Men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (1:21).
interpretation:
Peter greets those who have received “a faith of equal standing with ours,” which is to say the same faith that the apostles have, through the righteousness of “our God and Savior Jesus Christ.” Peter again calls Jesus God. Then he lays the foundation: “His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence, by which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire.” Everything we need has already been given. To be a “partaker of the divine nature” does not mean we become God. The best reading is that, by union with Christ, we share in his moral likeness and the life he gives, escaping the corruption of sin. We are reborn into a new life and will be made like him.

Since God has given everything, Peter urges effort: “For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge, and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness, and godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love.” It is a ladder of growth with faith at the base and love at the top. “For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The one who lacks them is nearsighted and has forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins. “Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent to make your calling and election sure, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall.” We do not make God’s election sure; we make it sure to us, confirming it by a transformed life. Then an entrance into the eternal kingdom will be supplied.

Peter then explains why he is writing. Soon he will die, and he wants them to remember these things. He does not rely on cleverly devised myths: “we were eyewitnesses of his majesty.” He was with Jesus on the mount of transfiguration and heard the voice from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.” That experience confirmed the Old Testament prophets’ message: “And we have something more sure, the prophetic word, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts.”

Finally, Peter tells us how to understand Scripture: “knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone’s own interpretation. For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.” The point is about the origin of Scripture, not about private reading. The writers were human, but the Holy Spirit carried them, as a ship is carried by wind, so what they wrote is God’s word. We examine this more on Day 851.
connection: Matthew 17:1-8 records the transfiguration that Peter witnessed. John 21:18-19 records Jesus’ prediction of Peter’s death. Romans 8:28-30 speaks of calling and election. Galatians 5:22-23 lists the fruit of the Spirit. Colossians 1:10 calls for growth in the knowledge of God. Titus 3:5-7 and 1 John 3:2 speak of new birth and being like Christ. Psalm 119:105 describes the word as a lamp. Revelation 22:16 calls Christ the bright morning star. 2 Timothy 3:16 speaks of the inspiration of Scripture. 2 Timothy 4:6-8 is Paul’s parallel farewell.
application:
Write out the seven qualities in verses 5 to 7 and rate yourself on each. Choose one to work on this week.

Memorize 1:3 and remind yourself that you already have everything you need for life and godliness in Christ.

Read the Bible today with a lamp-in-the-dark expectation: God will shed light on something.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for giving you everything you need for life and godliness.
Ask him to help you grow in virtue and knowledge.
Thank him for the prophetic word as a lamp.
